### 2026-10-06 – ## Week 1 – Designing the Starbie PCB

**6h**

## Week 1 – Designing the Starbie PCB

This was my first proper PCB design. I followed the Starbie guide: a 2-key desk pet with a XIAO ESP32-C3, a 0.96" SSD1306 OLED, an MPU6050 for tilt/shake, a DHT11 for temperature/humidity, and 2 Cherry MX switches. Here's how it went, including the places I got stuck.

### Setting up KiCad
Installed KiCad 10.0.6 on macOS and downloaded the care package. My first attempt at adding the libraries went wrong: I added the XIAO symbol library to the **Global** library table instead of the project one, and accidentally created an empty row that KiCad would have errored on. I cancelled, redid it under **Project Specific Libraries**, and made sure the paths used `${KIPRJMOD}`, so the libraries travel with the repo and anyone cloning it doesn't get "missing library" errors.

### Schematic
- Placed the XIAO and wired 5V/3.3V/GND, then used net labels (DHT, BTN1, BTN2, SDA, SCL) instead of long wires.
- **Stuck on labels:** my labels kept landing on top of the pin numbers and became unreadable.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/LHmsSD7oA5H8QaTGbxlIl4fooDz4pdTl/0ebb2b77389ec228a31d6debd376b4b4f5dfa187138ce6151bbfcaa9a129969b.png)

Rotating them got me vertical, stacked text. I fixed it by giving each label a short wire stub out from the pin and placing the label at the end of the stub.
- **Stuck on wires vs lines:** some of my "wires" were rendering a different colour from the others. Clicking each one and checking the Properties panel confirmed they were real wires, not graphic lines, which don't carry any connection.
- **Found a conflict in the guide:** its schematic image puts SCL on D4 and SDA on D5, but its own firmware pin table says SDA = D4 (GPIO6) and SCL = D5 (GPIO7). I kept the firmware-table version, since that's also the XIAO's default I2C mapping. Otherwise the firmware wouldn't talk to the OLED or MPU without editing.
- The OLED and MPU6050 share one I2C bus. Matched both connector pin orders against the guide's images and put no-connect flags on unused pins (MPU pins 5–8 and spare XIAO pins).
- The DHT11 is the bare 4-pin part, so it needs a 10k pull-up on the data line. Added R1 for that.
- Ran ERC: 3 "power pin not driven" errors, which come from USB power not being drawn in the schematic. They don't affect the board, so I left PWR_FLAGs for later.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/LHmsSD7oA5H8QaTGbxlIl4fooDz4pdTl/3765de1179c8d8f4a8869fcaba67066a3adf00e741472f0687f49d54590e34c1.png)

### Footprints
This took longer than expected. The Assign Footprints window's search filter didn't narrow the list for me, so I switched to setting each footprint directly in the symbol properties (E on each part). Halfway through I noticed the assignments had shifted onto the wrong parts: the XIAO had the resistor footprint, J2 had the XIAO footprint, and R1 had the DHT11's. I fixed them one by one, checking the reference designator each time before editing. The switches use Cherry MX footprints, which means I'll be buying MX switches and keycaps for the build, not tactile buttons.

### Layout
- Kept a rectangular board instead of the guide's star shape.
- **Problem 1:** the XIAO's USB-C port pointed straight at the DHT11, which would block the cable. Rotated the XIAO so USB faces the board edge and overhangs it slightly. The first outline left about 3 mm of board in front of the port, enough to block a USB-C plug, so I pulled the edge in to the connector.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/LHmsSD7oA5H8QaTGbxlIl4fooDz4pdTl/eb739e513820d7a737dea04f4285fe5d16fda9d507cce68f3c739f0feaa7d55b.png)
- **Problem 2:** J2 is only the header. The actual MPU6050 module plugs in and sticks out about 16 mm sideways. My first two DHT11 positions both sat inside that zone, so I moved the DHT11 down beside the XIAO.
- **Problem 3:** R1 sat on the edge of SW2's keycap outline. Nudged it clear.

### Routing
- At first I didn't understand what to do with the thin blue ratsnest lines. Each one is a connection that needs a real trace (except GND, which the pour handles). Routed the I2C and power lines first on F.Cu, then the long button traces on B.Cu so they could cross under the front traces.
- **Caught a short:** after zooming in, I found my DHT data trace ended on the DHT11's **3.3V pin** instead of the data pin, which would have shorted data to 3.3V. Deleted that path and rerouted it to pin 2.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/LHmsSD7oA5H8QaTGbxlIl4fooDz4pdTl/2cc29f179be295800a079f25a1880adda340c48a7c53b2c577149edb5ab85e96.png)
- **Ground pour:** first I accidentally picked the Rule Area tool, which makes a keep-out zone, not copper. Cancelled and used Place → Add Filled Zone instead, set to GND on both layers.

### DRC
- First run: 4 errors, 25 warnings, 1 unconnected item.
- Fixed a thermal-relief error on the OLED's GND pad: traces crowded it so only 1 spoke connected. Set the footprint's zone connection to Solid.
- **Stuck on a stub:** the unconnected item was a 0.26 mm piece of BTN2 track floating next to the XIAO pad. Clicking on the board kept selecting the GND pour instead, so I disabled zones in the selection filter. My first delete removed the wrong segment and made it 2 unconnected items. Undid that, and instead routed a short trace from the pad to the stub, which connected it properly.
- Final DRC: **0 unconnected**, and only the 2 "malformed courtyard" errors on the OLED footprint, which the guide says to ignore. The remaining warnings are silkscreen clipped at the board edge, from the intentional USB overhang.

![Screenshot 2026-10-07 at 03.07.26](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/LHmsSD7oA5H8QaTGbxlIl4fooDz4pdTl/425a6fab110b160619dffa8fc05a42cde41919380843fe5c7b9f726ef362e7f1.png)
### Outputs
Exported Gerbers and drill files, zipped them, and wrote the BOM. The BOM notes that the OLED must have GND-VCC-SCL-SDA pin order to match the footprint.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/LHmsSD7oA5H8QaTGbxlIl4fooDz4pdTl/e44cb7f9a9d3c997854585220878cbde5e260b9fdac77ae624c688a4315918bb.png)
**Next:** order parts and build it in week 6.

Time spent this session: 6 hours

### 2026-10-10 – ## October 9–10: Squarbie escapes KiCad and lands on GitHub!

**4h**

## October 9–10: Squarbie escapes KiCad and lands on GitHub!

The board was routed and DRC-clean, but it only existed on my laptop. This session was all about packaging it up: repo, BOM, README, and the progress reel. I thought this would be the "easy admin" part. It mostly was, until the terminal got involved.

**Cleaning up the folder first**

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/LHmsSD7oA5H8QaTGbxlIl4fooDz4pdTl/4594a26559e827fd4e0d5df7df34b00723ae0895c0292382caca438ee77c8bba.png)
Before putting anything on GitHub I listed the project folder, and it was full of stuff that has no business in a repo: KiCad lock files (`~Starbie1.kicad_pcb.lck` etc.), `.kicad_prl` (just my local view settings), macOS's `.DS_Store`, and a `.history` folder.

So I wrote a `.gitignore` to skip:
- KiCad backups, lock files, autosaves, and `fp-info-cache`
- `.kicad_prl`
- `.DS_Store` and `.history/`

The important catch was that I **didn't** ignore `fp-lib-table` and `sym-lib-table`. Those two files tell KiCad where my project-specific libraries live (the care-package parts in `lib/`). Leaving them out would mean anyone cloning the repo gets the exact "missing library" errors I went out of my way to avoid in entry 1.

**Writing the BOM (and realising I own zero tools)**

I wrote `BOM.md` straight from the footprints on the board: XIAO ESP32-C3, SSD1306 OLED, GY-521 MPU6050, bare 4-pin DHT11, 10k pull-up, 2× Cherry MX switches, keycaps, and the PCB itself. I added notes for the mistakes I can see week-6 me making:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/LHmsSD7oA5H8QaTGbxlIl4fooDz4pdTl/47bb76166ce6cb019ce4678a82e85a7958b1624ce4f0adb8c3df70d2bfb4e23f.png)
- The OLED has to be **GND-VCC-SCL-SDA** pin order. Some modules swap VCC and GND, and that would fry the screen.
- The DHT11 has to be the bare 4-pin part, not the 3-pin breakout, since the footprint and the pull-up resistor assume the bare one.

Then it hit me that I don't own a single tool. I worked out what the build actually needs: everything is through-hole, so a basic iron, solder, flux, and flush cutters are enough, and the hot plate and hot-air station are only for SMD. The [Half Life shop](https://halflife.hackclub.com/shop) has a basic soldering iron for 13 coins, and the bulletin confirmed tools come from the shop, not the grant. Solder, flux, and cutters aren't in the shop, so those will be a cheap local buy.

**Screenshots + README**

I cleared all the DRC markers first, because a PCB screenshot covered in yellow arrows isn't a great look. Then I took 4 shots: the routed PCB, the schematic, and two renders from KiCad's 3D viewer. This was the first time I saw Squarbie in 3D, and it suddenly looked like a real product. Weirdly emotional for a green rectangle.

They went into an `images/` folder, and the README shows the renders, a short description, and a guide to which file is what.

**Fighting GitHub (a little)**

I wanted to create the repo straight from the terminal using the [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com/). First attempt: zsh: command not found: gh

Cool. So:
- Installed it with `brew install gh`, which first decided to auto-update Homebrew and clean out a pile of old cache before doing what I asked.
- Ran `gh auth login`: picked HTTPS, logged in through the browser with a one-time code, and confirmed with `gh auth status`.
- Ran `git init` and `git add .`, then **checked `git status` before committing** to make sure none of the lock files or junk slipped through. The `.gitignore` did its job.
- Created the repo and pushed it in one command: `gh repo create squarbie --public --source=. --push`.
- Opened the repo page to check that the README and all 4 images actually render. They do!

Repo: https://github.com/Sagarpillai/squarbie

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/LHmsSD7oA5H8QaTGbxlIl4fooDz4pdTl/425bc833d33daf6323c903f4cc0bde39cb8062dc2916dc08cc49e90d003984f5.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/LHmsSD7oA5H8QaTGbxlIl4fooDz4pdTl/9f26f0017bccec8a8545a6ac77db61215a51529351af510759b4c976a5ac0eaa.png)

**Progress reel**

The reel prompt was "narrate one decision you reversed". Easy pick: the DHT11 placement. First it blocked the XIAO's USB-C port, then I moved it right where the MPU6050 module overhangs its header, and on the third try it finally landed beside the XIAO, clear of everything. I recorded the PCB and 3D view while explaining that.

**tl;dr:** Squarbie now has a clean repo (with a proper `.gitignore` that keeps the library tables), a BOM with notes so I don't fry the OLED, a README with 3D renders, and a reel. The board is ready to submit.

Time spent this session: 4 hours
